title: A Shower Remodel Inspired a Cleaner, Cheaper Way to Extract Lithium
summary: The race for lithium — the silvery metal that powers everything from smartphones to electric vehicles — has a dirty secret. Most of it comes from either sprawling evaporation ponds in South American deserts or energy-guzzling hard-rock mines that roast ore at 1,000°C and douse it in sulfuric acid. But a team at MIT, inspired by a 25-year-old bathroom renovation, has unveiled a cleaner, potentially cheaper alternative. The key ingredient? Ammonium fluoride, a weak acid found in common glass-etching cream. “I was remodeling a shower in Framingham, Massachusetts, about 25 years ago,” recalls Yet-Ming Chiang, an MIT professor and serial entrepreneur. “When we started this project, I remembered that glass etching cream and thought, ‘What’s in that?’” The answer led to a breakthrough published in Science. The researchers found that under the right conditions, ammonium fluoride can dissolve stubborn silicate minerals like spodumene — the primary lithium ore — without producing hydrofluoric acid, a notoriously dangerous chemical. The process runs in simple stirred plastic tanks at just 95°C (200°F). In under 12 hours, it leaches out nearly all the lithium, along with valuable byproducts: alumina for aluminum smelting and cementitious silica for concrete. The acid can be recycled in a closed loop. Chiang calls it “nose-to-tail” mining — using every part of the ore. A startup called Rock Zero, co-founded by study first author Benjamin Mowbray, is now racing to commercialize the technology. The team has designed a pilot plant and aims to begin construction by the end of 2026, with operations starting in 2027. Their cost models project lithium extraction at under $6,000 per metric ton — competitive with brine and cheaper than conventional hard-rock processing. If successful, the method could unlock vast, previously uneconomical lithium reserves and slash the carbon footprint of battery production. Not bad for an idea that started in a shower stall.
why_it_matters: As you charge your phone or ride in an electric car, the lithium inside likely came from a mine that damaged ecosystems and used huge amounts of energy — this new method could make the batteries of the future far cleaner and cheaper, directly affecting the planet you'll inherit.

background_read: Lithium is essential for the lithium-ion batteries that power smartphones, laptops, and electric vehicles. Most of the world's lithium currently comes from two sources: huge evaporation ponds in the salt flats of South America (especially in Chile, Argentina, and Bolivia) and hard-rock mines, primarily in Australia, that cook spodumene ore at over 1,000°C and treat it with sulfuric acid.

The evaporation pond method consumes enormous amounts of water in already arid regions, harming local communities and flamingo habitats. Hard-rock mining has a high carbon footprint and produces toxic waste. Both approaches have drawn criticism from environmental groups and have led to a search for less damaging extraction methods.

Yet-Ming Chiang is a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) who previously co-founded several battery startups, including A123 Systems and Form Energy. His sudden inspiration during a bathroom remodel to try ammonium fluoride came after 25 years — showing how scientific breakthroughs often arise from seemingly unrelated everyday experiences.

The concept of a 'closed-loop' process, where chemicals are recycled rather than discarded, is a growing trend in green chemistry. If Rock Zero's pilot plant succeeds, it could dramatically reduce both the carbon emissions and the chemical waste associated with lithium production, potentially making electric vehicles even cleaner.

perspectives.description: If the ammonium fluoride method works at scale, it could sharply reduce the water use, carbon emissions, and toxic acid spills that plague current lithium mining. It also turns waste into sellable materials like concrete additive and alumina, making the whole operation more profitable and less wasteful.

Scaling up from a laboratory success to a full industrial plant always brings surprises — the acid recycling may be less efficient in practice, or the byproducts might not find a reliable market. There is also a risk that cheaper lithium could accelerate battery consumption without solving the social and environmental problems in mining regions.

Lithium is often called 'white gold' because a handful of countries control most of the supply. A new process that works on lower-grade ores could shift that balance, reducing dependency on a few nations and making domestic extraction feasible in places like the United States, which holds its own spodumene reserves.

If Rock Zero's pilot plant proves the method can deliver cheap, clean lithium by 2027, the mining industry might quickly adopt ammonium fluoride leaching for other hard-to-process minerals. That could spark a wave of 'urban mining' — extracting lithium from old batteries — using similar mild chemistry to close the loop on battery recycling.
